blocks.text: **Hairy cell leukemia (Option D):** is a chronic B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder, and peripheral smear findings typically demonstrate the presence of small, Mature lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm and "hairy" projections.

items.text: **CD20 (Option A):** is a surface marker present on most B cells and is commonly expressed in a variety of B-cell lymphomas and leukemias. While CD20 can be positive, it is not specific to HCL and is found in many other B-cell neoplasms.
**Annexin A5 (Option B):** is a protein involved in the cellular processes related to apoptosis and phospholipid binding. It is used as a marker to detect apoptotic cells.
**Apolipoprotein A1 (Option D):** is a marker for germ cell neoplasms.

blocks.text: In the above case, the patient is from a non-endemic region, and the lesion mainly affects the abdomen. Based on the HPE and IHC findings, it is suggestive of sporadic Burkitt’s lymphoma. Burkitt's lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma associated with the translocations of the c-MYC gene on chromosome 8, t(8:14).
It has three primary subtypes:

items.text: Endemic Burkitt's lymphoma: Commonly affects children in malaria-endemic areas of Africa, often presenting with tumours in the jaw or facial bones. (Option A)
Sporadic Burkitt's lym phoma: More frequently seen in non-endemic regions and usually involving the ileocaecal region and peritoneum. (Option B)
Immunodeficiency-associated Burkitt's lymphoma: Found in patients with conditions such as HIV/AIDS or other forms of immunodeficiency. (Option C).

blocks.text: The given scenario, along with HPE and IHC, is consistent with Follicular lymphoma, which is associated with BCL2- gene translocation; t(14:18) Follicular lymphoma (FL) is a malignant neoplasm originating from germinal center B-cells, characterized by the t(14;18) translocation leading to overexpression of BCL2. Clinically, it presents with painless lymphadenopathy and may include systemic symptoms.

Histopathologically, FL exhibits a nodular growth pattern with centrocytes (Small cells with cleaved nuclei and scanty cytosol) and centroblasts(Larger cells with open nuclear chromatin, several nucleoli) Immunohistochemistry shows positivity for CD10/19/20, BCL2, and BCL6, and negativity for CD5. Management focuses on palliative approaches due to its indolent but incurable nature.

items.text: **Follicular hyperplasia (Option A):** is benign, featuring reactive B cell proliferation in lymph nodes with preserved architecture, characterized by CD10/20 positivity and absence of BCL2 expression.

**Mantle cell lymphoma (Option B):** Immunohistochemistry shows positivity for Cyclin D1, CD19, CD20, surface immunoglobulins (usually IgM and IgD), and CD5, but CD23 is negative and HPE shows small lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear outlines, condensed chromatin, and scanty cytoplasm

Burkitt’s lymphoma (Option D) Histopathological examination reveals numerous mitotic and apoptotic cells, nuclear remnants phagocytosed by benign macrophages with abundant clear cytoplasm, creating a characteristic "starry sky" pattern. Immunohistochemistry shows positivity for IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL6, but negativity for BCL2.

blocks.text: The clinical presentation with mandibular mass and a starry sky appearance on HPE are characteristic of Burkitt’s lymphoma, which is associated with the translocation of the MYC gene on chromosome 8, thus leading to overexpression of the MYC protein. All forms of Burkitt’s lymphoma (Endemic, Sporadic and HIV associated) are associated with such translocations. The most common translocations are t (8:2), t(8:14), and t(8:22).

items.text: **BCL2 gene (Option B):** translocation is associated with follicular lymphoma. The most common is t(14;18), leading to the juxtaposition of the IGH locus (Ch 14) with the BCL2 locus(Ch 18), leading to overexpression of BCL2.

**Cyclin-D1 (Option C):** gene translocation is associated with all mantle cell lymphoma. There is a translocation of the cyclin D1 locus on chromosome 11 and IGH locus on chromosome 14; t(11;14), which results in overexpression of cyclin D1, thus promoting G1 to S-phase progression in the cell cycle.
**BCL6 gene (Option D):** dysregulation is associated with Diffuse large B cell lymphoma. It can occur due to translocations or promoter sequence mutations of the BCL6 gene on Chr. 3q27.

blocks.title: Clinical Staging of Hodgkins Lymphoma (Ann Arbor Classification)
rows: Involvement of a single lymph node region (I) or a single extra lymphatic organ or site (IE).
Involvement of two or more lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm alone (II) or localised involvement of an extra lymphatic organ or site (IIE).
Involvement of lymph node regions on both sides of the diaphragm without (III) or with (IIIE) localised involvement of an extra lymphatic organ or site.
Diffuse involvement of one or more extra lymphatic organs or sites with or without lymphatic involvement.

blocks.text: All stages are further divided based on the absence (A) or presence (B) of the following symptoms: unexplained fever, drenching night sweats, and/or unexplained weight loss of greater than 10% of normal body weight.

Predominant (Non-Classical) Hodgkin Lymphoma: Histological Features: Predominant (Non-Classical) Hodgkin Lymphoma is characterised by large, atypical cells with prominent nucleoli and a mixed inflammatory background. Immunophenotype: The atypical cells in this subtype typically lack expression of CD15 and CD30 but are positive for CD20 and CD45 markers, distinct from classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

Clinical Presentation: painless lymphadenopathy, fever, night sweats, and weight loss, similar to classical Hodgkin lymphoma Prognosis: overall survival rates may be lower compared to classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Epidemiology: Less common than classical Hodgkin lymphoma and may occur in younger and older adults.

items.text: **CD3 (Option B):** is a marker of mature T lymphocytes and is not typically expressed by the large, atypical cells seen in Predominant (Non-Classical) Hodgkin’s lymphoma

CD15 and CD 30 (Option C) and (Option D) are markers commonly expressed on Reed-Sternberg cells in classical Hodgkin's lymphoma but is typically negative in predominantly (Non-Classical) Hodgkin’s lymphoma

blocks.text: Lymphocyte-depleted Hodgkin's lymphoma Histological Features: LDHL is characterised by a scarcity of lymphocytes and many pleomorphic, often bizarre Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells. The cellular environment is typically rich in fibrosis or necrosis. Immunophenotype: The RS cells in LDHL are usually positive for CD15 and CD30 but negative for CD20.

Clinical Presentation: systemic symptoms such as fever, night sweats, and significant weight loss referred to as "B symptoms.” Epidemiology: LDHL is the least common subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma and is more frequently diagnosed in older adults and individuals with HIV infection.

Prognosis: LDHL is associated with a poorer prognosis compared to other Hodgkin lymphoma subtypes due to its more aggressive nature Treatment: Treatment typically involves a combination of chemotherapy and, in some cases, radiation therapy..

items.text: Presence of fibrous bands (Option A) it is characteristic of nodular sclerosis Hodgkin's lymphoma, not LDHL. Nodular sclerosis is marked by the presence of fibrous bands that divide the lymph node into nodules.

**Abundance of reactive lymphocytes (Option B):** it is typical of lymphocyte-rich Hodgkin's lymphoma, a subtype characterised by an abundance of small, reactive lymphocytes and relatively few Reed-Sternberg cells.

**Predominance of nodular growth pattern (Option D):** it is associated with nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma (NLPHL), not LDHL. It is characterised by a nodular growth pattern and the presence of "popcorn" or lymphocyte-predominant cells,

blocks.text: Nodular Lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma; Histological Features: Nodular Lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma is characterised by a predominance of reactive lymphocytes with relatively few Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells. Immunophenotype: The RS cells are typically positive for CD20 and negative for CD15 and CD30, distinguishing it from other subtypes of Hodgkin lymphoma.

Clinical Presentation: Patients often present with painless lymphadenopathy, commonly in peripheral lymph nodes rather than mediastinal involvement. Prognosis: This subtype generally has a favourable prognosis compared to other types of Hodgkin lymphoma due to its lower aggressiveness and higher responsiveness to treatment.

items.text: **Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma (Option A):** is the most common subtype, characterised by the presence of lacunar Reed-Sternberg cells and fibrous bands that divide the lymphoid tissue into nodules. These cells are usually positive for CD15 and CD30 but negative for CD20.

**Mixed cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma (Option B):** features a heterogeneous mixture of cells, including Reed-Sternberg cells, lymphocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils, and plasma cells. These cells are typically CD15 and CD30 positive but negative for CD20.

**Lymphocyte-depleted Hodgkin lymphoma (Option D):** is the least common subtype and is characterised by a paucity of lymphocytes and a high number of pleomorphic, often bizarre Reed-Sternberg cells. These cells are usually CD15 and CD30 positive but negative for CD20 and associated with a poorer prognosis

blocks.text: Mixed Cellularity Hodgkin’s Lymphoma often presents at an advanced stage (III or IV), which is generally associated with a worse prognosis compared to the Nodular Sclerosis subtype, which typically presents at an earlier stage (I or II) and has a relatively better prognosis.

items.text: Mixed-Cellularity Hodgkin Lymphoma (MCHL) accounts for 20% to 25% of cases and features lymph nodes diffusely effaced by a heterogeneous cellular infiltrate, including T cells, eosinophils, plasma cells, and macrophages, along with abundant Reed-Sternberg and mononuclear variants. (Option A)
Approximately 70% of Reed-Sternberg cells are EBV-positive. (Option B)
RS cells are CD15+, CD30+ (Option C)
MCHL is more prevalent in males and is more likely to be associated with systemic symptoms such as night sweats and weight loss.

blocks.text: The given clinical scenario points towards diagnosing Nodular Sclerosis type of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma which features characteristic Lacunar variant Reed-Sternberg cells and collagen deposition in lymph nodes. Its background includes T cells, eosinophils, plasma cells, and macrophages, with occasional diagnostic Reed-Sternberg cells, which express PAX5, CD15, and CD30.

Spread may involve spleen, liver, and bone marrow, infrequently associated with Epstein-Barr virus. Occurring equally in males and females, it commonly affects lower cervical, supraclavicular, and mediastinal lymph nodes in adolescents or young adults and has an excellent prognosis.

items.text: Nodular Lymphocyte-Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma ( Option B) is characterised by a background of follicular dendritic cells and reactive B cells, with frequent lymphocyte-rich (Popcorn cell) variants, typically does not express CD15 or CD30 and is usually EBV-negative.

Lymphocyte-Rich Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma ( Option C) is characterised by a background infiltrate rich in T lymphocytes, with frequent mononuclear and diagnostic RS cells. RS cells of this type typically express CD15 and CD30 and are usually EBV-negative.

Lymphocyte-Depleted Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma ( Option D) has a paucity of background reactive cells and frequent diagnostic RS cells. RS cells in lymphocyte-depleted classical Hodgkin lymphoma typically express CD15 and CD30 and are usually EBV-positive. It often presents with advanced disease.
